newsitem.title: USA: Black & Decker's profits plunge on lower sales.
newsitem.headline: Black & Decker's profits plunge on lower sales.

text.p: Black & Decker Corp. said Friday its profit plunged by 31 percent in the first quarter as sales slipped 5 percent, primarily due to lower demand for the company's "SnakeLight" flexible flashlights

The manufacturer of hand and power tools for consumers and professionals said its net income for the three months ended March 30 fell to $26.3 million, or 27 cents a share, from $38 million, or 39 cents a share.

It added that its sales declined to $1.01 billion from $1.06 billion, mainly due to decreased demand for its flexible flashlights by retailers -- who had rushed to stock up on the new product a year ago.

"SnakeLight sales were substantially lower than last year, reflecting adequate retail inventories of this product during the first quarter of 1997 compared to the same period last year, when retailers were aggressively filling their pipelines," Chairman Nolan D. Archibald said in a statement.
"The SnakeLight sales decline also was the primary contributor to a decline in operating income for the corporation during the quarter."
The company added, however, that, excluding the effects of foreign currency translation, sales declined by only 2 percent.
Black & Decker, which is based in Towson, Md., also said a higher income tax rate this year hurt its earnings for the quarter.

"Having used most of the remaining benefits of our domestic net operating losses in 1996 ... our tax rate climbed from an effective rate of 27 percent last year to 35 percent," it said. "This anticipated increase in our tax rate had a significant negative impact on our earnings for the quarter."
Black & Decker's stock was unchanged at $29.875 in early trading on the New York Stock Exchange.
